So I was recently watching this Jimquisition episode about the new Deus Ex, and how the microtransactions were disabled during the review period of the game, and then turned on for release. This lead reviewers to completely ignore the effect of what amounted to purchasable progress of the RPG mechanics. Jim further expressed concern that the game might be updated down the line to mathematically funnel you towards needing to purchase these boosts to complete the game.

And I feel like every few weeks there is a new controversy surrounding games being updated in a way that's anti consumer. Payday 2 adding crazy bullshit microtransactions. CS:GO getting a crazy bullshit weapons update that breaks the game. Electronic Arts pulling a bunch of servers offline annually, so you can never play those games again. Fuck, I'd just gotten Darkspore in a bundle when they took that down. Never even had a chance to try it. Sometimes even broadly perceived positive changes alienate people, like Evolve's hail mary overhaul, or Diablo 3 gutting the auction house and completely redoing the loot system. Anybody who bought into the old system is now SOL and feels like a chump.

And it's easy to lash out at each individual problem, and not notice the root cause.

We no longer own our games. Games are thoroughly entrenched in the "Software as a Service" paradigm.

Back in the 90's, we really owned the software we purchased. Almost every game you purchased allowed you to modify it however you wanted, run whatever patch version you wanted, and play locally or online without any centralized servers snapping a ruler against your knuckles for being a naughty boy. Hell, sometimes if a patch for a game sucked bad enough, people wouldn't install it! I recall this happening a few times for the original Counter-Strike mod.

And even now, if I wanted, I can install the version of Diablo 2 I played all summer long as a teenager, and recreate my stupid bow wielding Necromancer. I can't do that with Diablo 3. I could call up my old friends, and we could rock out in Quake 1 with the Team Fortress mod exactly like we remember it. We can't do that with the version of Team Fortress 2 we first played.

It's been about 10 years since this really began in earnest, and I really worry about how much of our heritage as gamers has been wiped out. How many games from our past, and the specific versions we may remember so fondly on launch day after months of youthful hype, are simply extinct?

I wonder if we'll look back on this era in gaming the way we look back on Silent Film.

Self-hosting and connecting to specific IP addresses is still around in some capacity at least; see the likes of Killing Floor 2 and Starbound. A lot of games also support it indirectly by including a LAN option (such as the Borderlands series), in that it would be at least possible (at worst) to play using network virtualisation if the matchmaking/community server goes down and there's no direct IP option in the interface. If any developer is thoughtful enough to release the server software to customers when they take down their official server, that could be worth supporting too.

Incidentally, one commercial aspect of withholding the server component of a software product in general is that, since the server isn't being distributed, it becomes possible to use GPL libraries to construct it without incurring any obligation to publish the source code, or indeed to use proprietry libraries without needing to pay for a distribution license.
